Scoring Explanations Without Reading Them: Structural Shortcuts in
Automated-Interpretability Evaluation Data

Xupeng Chen Affiliation: Dimension Gate Correspondence to: xc1490@nyu.edu
Abstract

Automated interpretability scores an explanation of a sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature by asking a model to predict, token by token, where the feature fires on evaluation examples or to judge whether marked tokens fit it. We find that the evaluation data standard pipelines build can be scored without reading the explanation. On Neuronpedia’s stored fuzzing runs for 500 random GPT-2 small features, 91.3% of activating examples are cropped with the peak on the centre token, and a rule that says “yes” when the centre token is marked reaches balanced accuracy 0.979, against 0.838 for the stored LLM scorers (recomputed from the stored per-item verdicts, on marks rebuilt from the pipeline’s code); a rule reading only the mark count reaches 0.969. The cue changes form across pipelines: current delphi always marks the same slot in its fuzzing negatives, and full-context runs mark negatives with more tokens. OpenAI’s simulation benchmark lists each neuron’s top-activating sequences first; a rule that predicts activity on the first five scores 0.227 in pooled correlation against 0.160 for GPT-4’s published simulator (post hoc). We give closed forms for what such rules can score; show that one scorer’s simulation scores are higher on stored snippets than on natural windows but not shown to be reordered; and build windows that remove the position cue, derive but do not build negatives that remove the mark cues, and separate the sequence cue by decomposition. On natural-text windows cut at random offsets, the best fixed-offset prior shared by all features scores 0.015. On them, that scorer, a typed decision model (Jev), reaches a pooled correlation of 0.331 over 49 features, against 0.013 with shuffled explanations, and an open 8B simulator with the original read-out reads the explanation there (0.194 against 0.019). Scores should be reported beside the best explanation-free rule on the same items.

Keywords: 
automated interpretability, sparse autoencoders, evaluation, shortcuts

1 Introduction

Open a GPT-2 small (Radford et al., 2019) SAE feature on Neuronpedia (Lin, 2023) and look at a fuzzing run stored for it. Its twenty activating examples are 17-token windows cut around the feature’s strongest activation, so the peak sits on the ninth token; its five non-activating examples carry marks placed by a seeded sampler. The scorer, an LLM, reads the explanation and each example with some tokens marked, and answers whether the marked tokens are what the explanation describes (Paulo et al., 2025). A rule that never reads the explanation and answers “yes” whenever the ninth token is marked is right on almost every item. For 500 random features and 1,001 stored runs, that rule reaches balanced accuracy 0.979 against 0.838 for the stored LLM scorers (recomputed from their stored per-item verdicts). The runs do not store which tokens were marked, so these marks are rebuilt from the current code of the scorer fork (version inferred, Appendix D); a rule reading only the number of marks, which does not depend on the inferred seed, reaches 0.969. These scores are what SAE papers and benchmarks use to compare dictionaries and explainers (Paulo et al., 2025; Karvonen et al., 2025).

The construction of an example (where it is cropped, which tokens are marked and how many, which sequences are drawn from the top of the activation distribution) carries information about the answer that a rule can read without the explanation. We examine four public pipelines, three of which carry a cue a rule can read, and our own control (Figures 1 and 2): the position of the peak in cropped windows; fixed mark positions and mark counts in fuzzing negatives, which survive in current delphi (EleutherAI, 2024) and in Neuronpedia’s newer full-context runs; and sequence membership in the top-and-random sets that simulation scores are computed on (Bills et al., 2023), where a rule that predicts activity on the first five sequences of OpenAI’s files (post hoc) scores 0.227 in pooled correlation, and an oracle given each sequence’s mean activation 0.288, against 0.160 for GPT-4’s published simulator. Each cue has a closed form or a sharp bound (Section 3); the position cue is removed by a construction we build, the mark cues by one we derive, and the sequence cue is separated by a decomposition (Section 6).

Whether the cue changes conclusions is a separate question. We test it with one scorer, Jev, a commercial typed decision model, which returns a distribution over declared answer options instead of generating text (Almeida, 2026). Its simulation scores are higher on stored snippets than on natural windows for 44 of 49 features (a comparison that also changes window length and composition); a preregistered test finds them tracking crop geometry but does not show the cue reordering features (Spearman 0.732 between the two sets). In the few stored fuzzing items where the centre cue and the answer disagree (16 per scorer, on rebuilt marks), the LLM scorers rarely followed the cue, although their per-feature accuracy rises with a mark-count rule’s (Section 5). A score is evidence about an explanation only if the scorer beats every explanation-free rule on the same items; on natural windows Jev scores 0.331 against 0.013 for a shuffled explanation, above every position prior and the sequence-level oracle, and mostly within sequences; an open-weight 8B simulator with the original read-out also reads the explanation there (0.194 against 0.019). On OpenAI’s benchmark, where that oracle exceeds both GPT-4’s published simulator and Jev, the same decomposition shows that Jev’s lead over GPT-4 lies mostly between sequences (Section 7).

Contributions.

  1. 1.

    Three structural cues in four public pipelines. Peak position in Neuronpedia’s stored crops (500 random features; centre rule 0.979 against stored scorers’ 0.838 on rebuilt marks), fixed mark positions and mark counts in fuzzing negatives (current delphi, Neuronpedia’s full-context runs), and sequence order in top-and-random simulation sets, with closed forms for what such rules can score (Sections 3 and 4, Figure 2).

  2. 2.

    A preregistered ranking test, and a level difference beside it. One scorer’s simulation scores are higher on stored snippets than on natural windows (post hoc; the sets also differ in length and composition), and the preregistered test does not show the cue reordering features; the few stored fuzzing items that could reveal use of the centre cue (16 per scorer) show no sign of it. A small scorer trained on the stored snippets loses 63% of its score on natural windows, and the same architecture trained with no explanation at all reaches 83% of its held-out score (Section 5).

  3. 3.

    Constructions for each cue, and a scorer that clears them. Random-offset natural windows remove the position cue (stitching only relocates it; local activations match the public ones only with the BOS token); matched marks remove the mark cues (derived, not built); rwr_{w} separates the sequence cue. Jev beats every explanation-free rule on natural windows, and an open 8B simulator beats its shuffled control there but not the per-feature offset oracle; Jev’s pooled lead over GPT-4’s published simulator is mostly between sequences (Sections 6 and 7).

2 Related Work

Explaining and scoring units automatically.

Unit description began in vision (Bau et al., 2017; Hernandez et al., 2022; Oikarinen & Weng, 2023); Bills et al. (2023) introduced explain-then-simulate for language-model neurons, and SAE work adopted the same loop to label dictionary features (Cunningham et al., 2024; Bricken et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024). Paulo et al. (2025) scaled it to millions of features and added detection and fuzzing, released as delphi (EleutherAI, 2024; Juang et al., 2024); Neuronpedia runs a fork of that code and stores its runs (Lin, 2023). Other work fine-tunes explainers and simulators (Choi et al., 2024), improves explanations (Singh et al., 2023; Gur-Arieh et al., 2025) or lets agents run experiments (Shaham et al., 2024); we keep explainers and scorers fixed.

Evaluating explanation scores and SAEs.

A high simulation score can coexist with an explanation that misses a unit’s causal role (Huang et al., 2023). Explanations have been checked on functions with known descriptions (Schwettmann et al., 2023), generated concept data (Kopf et al., 2024) and sanity checks (Oikarinen et al., 2025); the metrics score SAEs on random transformers well (Heap et al., 2026), FADE separates failure modes (Puri et al., 2025), and explanations depend on the data used to find top activations (Bolukbasi et al., 2021). Benchmarks add task-based evaluation of SAEs (Makelov et al., 2025; Karvonen et al., 2025; Kantamneni et al., 2025), and Paulo & Belrose (2026) evaluate SAE interpretability without explanations at all. van der Ben et al. (2026) find that pipeline settings (corpus, example draws) move scores more than architecture does and change top-kk feature rankings. These studies vary the explanation, model, task or settings; we hold them fixed and measure what the construction of the items alone lets a rule score (our ranking comparison, Section 5, is one scorer’s rank correlation between two data sets, not top-kk stability across draws).

Shortcuts and leakage in evaluation data.

Benchmarks often admit solutions that ignore the intended signal: hypothesis-only baselines and annotation artifacts (Poliak et al., 2018; Gururangan et al., 2018), syntactic heuristics (McCoy et al., 2019), shortcut learning (Geirhos et al., 2020), saliency maps that ignore the model (Adebayo et al., 2018), and leakage (Kapoor & Narayanan, 2023). Our explanation-free rules are input-only baselines whose input is the construction of the item rather than its text, so they have closed forms.

The first position of a transformer.

The first token acts as an attention sink (Xiao et al., 2024) with very large residual values (Sun et al., 2024), and some units are purely positional (Voita et al., 2024); an SAE trained with a beginning-of-sequence token and applied without one reads the first real token as that outlier.

Typed decision models and cheap judges.

LLMs serve as annotators and judges (Gilardi et al., 2023; Ziems et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2023), with position biases (Wang et al., 2024); cost-aware systems route easy queries to cheaper models (Chen et al., 2024; Ding et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025), and encoders score predefined options cloze-style (Schick & Schütze, 2021; Devlin et al., 2019; Warner et al., 2025; Marone et al., 2026). Typed decision models (Section 1): Ibrahim & Zaki (2026) find them cheaper and less accurate than frontier LLMs for annotation, Laya is an open implementation (Convai Innovations, 2026), and Sun et al. (2026) show that such a head can follow an option’s name instead of its rubric. Calibration depends on model and format (Guo et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2021; Kadavath et al., 2022); Proposition 1(a) states what correlation scoring requires.

3 Problem Setup

Simulation.

A feature is scored on sequences s=1,…,ms=1,\dots,m with tokens t=1,…,nst=1,\dots,n_{s} and true activations as​ta_{st}; N=∑snsN=\sum_{s}n_{s}. A simulator reads the explanation ee and returns a^s​t\hat{a}_{st} for every token, and the score is the Pearson correlation over all tokens pooled, as in OpenAI’s released code (Bills et al., 2023):

r⁡(a,a^)=∑s,t(as​t−a¯)​(a^s​t−a^¯)[∑s,t(as​t−a¯)2]1/2​[∑s,t(a^s​t−a^¯)2]1/2.r(a,\hat{a})=\frac{\sum_{s,t}(a_{st}-\bar{a})(\hat{a}_{st}-\bar{\hat{a}})}{\big[\sum_{s,t}(a_{st}-\bar{a})^{2}\big]^{1/2}\big[\sum_{s,t}(\hat{a}_{st}-\bar{\hat{a}})^{2}\big]^{1/2}}. (1)

Fuzzing and detection.

An item xx is a window, positive if the feature is active on it and negative otherwise, with a set of marked token positions M⁡(x)M(x). Fuzzing asks whether the marked tokens are instances of ee; detection shows the window unmarked and asks whether any token is (Paulo et al., 2025). A verdict g⁡(x)∈{0,1}g(x)\in\{0,1\} is scored by balanced accuracy

BA(g)=12(Pr+[g=1]+Pr−[g=0]),\mathrm{BA}(g)=\tfrac{1}{2}\big(\Pr_{+}[g=1]+\Pr_{-}[g=0]\big), (2)

with Pr±\Pr_{\pm} over the positive and negative items.

Explanation-free rules and the estimand.

A rule is explanation-free if it is a function of the item’s construction alone: token positions, the mark set M⁡(x)M(x), and which sequence a token belongs to, but not ee and not the text. For a scorer ff and a pre-specified family 𝒢\mathcal{G} of such rules evaluated on the same items, we report the pair

(score⁡(f),maxg∈𝒢⁡score⁡(g)),\big(\mathrm{score}(f),\ \max_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\mathrm{score}(g)\big), (3)

and call a score evidence about ee only when the first exceeds the second and a shuffled explanation brings ff down to or below it. The families we use are the fixed-position priors (1 at one token index, 0 elsewhere), the centre-marked and fixed-slot mark rules, and the count rule “yes iff |M⁡(x)||M(x)| differs from the negatives’ mark count”. Beside them we report, as a ceiling rather than a rule, the sequence-mean oracle a^s​t=a¯s\hat{a}_{st}=\bar{a}_{s}, which uses the true sequence means and bounds every rule that is constant within sequences (Proposition 1(c)). Rules chosen after seeing the data are flagged as optimistic.

Three closed forms.

Known results (Robinson, 1950; Tate, 1954; Lehmann & Romano, 2005) in the form we use; proofs are in Appendix B.

4 Three Cues in Four Public Pipelines

Data.

We measured the evaluation data of four public pipelines and of our own control (Appendix D). (i) Neuronpedia’s stored fuzzing runs for the residual-stream SAE on GPT-2 small layer 8 (Bloom, 2024), the only SAE with stored runs at scale that we found: 500 features drawn at random (the 500-feature sample), with 1,001 runs by LLM scorers (Gemini Team, 2024; Grattafiori et al., 2024) (500 by gemini-2.0-flash, 2025-02, 500 by llama-3.1-70b-instruct, 2025-03, and 1 by claude-3.5-sonnet), plus the first 50 features in index order, which we also scored ourselves; and every Gemma-2-2B (Gemma Team, 2024) layer-20 Gemma Scope feature (Lieberum et al., 2024) among indices 0–1,199 that carries a stored run: 12 features, 27 newer runs (2025-08 to 2026-03). (ii) Examples built locally for the 50 features with the example constructor and fuzzing sampler of delphi (EleutherAI/delphi at commit 4fea06e), in its default mode and with centring enabled; (iii) SAEBench’s scoring windows, built the same way. (iv) The 400 GPT-2 XL neurons we sampled from OpenAI’s release, which provides for each neuron GPT-4’s (OpenAI, 2023) explanation, its top-and-random scoring sequences, the true activations and GPT-4’s per-token simulations (Bills et al., 2023). (v) As a control, natural windows we built (Section 6). Stored runs keep each item’s text, activations and the scorer’s verdict but not which tokens were marked. Stored accuracies below are recomputed from those verdicts; the score Neuronpedia displays differs from this recomputation on 112 of the 1,001 runs (its mean is 0.845 against 0.838), and the centre rule is above the displayed score on 735 runs and below it on 89. Neuronpedia’s server still runs a fork of delphi’s predecessor, sae-auto-interp; we rebuild the marks with that fork’s rule (positives: every token at or above 0.3 of the item’s maximum; negatives: a sample of fixed size drawn after resetting the seed to 22; the version is inferred, Appendix D). Every fuzzing-rule number on stored runs is on these rebuilt marks, but only the negatives’ mark positions depend on the inferred seed: positives’ marks and the negatives’ mark count follow from the stored activations, and the count rule does not use positions. With the negatives’ positions drawn uniformly at random instead (post hoc, exact expectation), the centre rule scores 0.880 against the stored scorers’ 0.838, higher on 523 of 1,001 runs (p=0.16p=0.16). The 500-feature, fuzzing-rule, delphi and SAEBench analyses and the harm test were preregistered with decision rules (Appendix E); the centre prior and η\eta on the 50 stored-snippet features and the 400 OpenAI neurons predate them, and post hoc analyses are marked. Unless stated otherwise, pp-values are two-sided sign tests over runs, features or neurons, not adjusted for multiple comparisons.

Position: peak-centred crops.

Neuronpedia’s stored examples are 17-token windows centred on the activation peak: over the 500 random features, 91.3% of activating examples peak on the centre token. A simulator that predicts 1 on the centre token and 0 elsewhere reaches a mean pooled correlation of 0.732, and the best fixed index, chosen after the fact, 0.760. In fuzzing, the rebuilt positive marks almost always include the centre and the fixed-seed negative marks almost never do, so the rule “yes iff the centre token is marked” reaches balanced accuracy 0.979 on rebuilt marks, above both stored scorers on the same runs: gemini-2.0-flash 0.864 (the rule wins on 312 runs and loses on 59, p=1.1×10−42p=1.1\times 10^{-42}) and llama-3.1-70b 0.812 (437 to 23, p=2.7×10−100p=2.7\times 10^{-100}). On the first 50 features (Table 3) the same rule reaches 0.985 against 0.790, 0.858 and 0.841 for llama-3.1-70b, gemini-1.5-flash and gemini-2.0-flash (sign tests p≤4.1×10−5p\leq 4.1\times 10^{-5}), and the centre prior 0.723, which Proposition 2 reproduces per feature to 10−1410^{-14} (an algebraic identity on the same data); the centre token carries on average 68% of each feature’s activation mass there. The Gemma runs, by contrast, use 127-token windows with the peak anywhere: the centre prior is 0.003 and the centre rule 0.552 on rebuilt marks.

Marks: fixed positions and counts in fuzzing negatives.

The fork marks each negative with nn tokens, where nn is the mean number of active tokens on the positives rounded up (active tokens outnumber the tokens at or above 0.3 of the maximum that positives mark), at positions drawn after resetting the seed, so negatives are marked at the same slots and with more marks than positives carry: 3.6 against 1.9 on the GPT-2 runs, 19.9 against 9.2 on the Gemma runs. On the Gemma runs the count rule reaches 0.981 on rebuilt marks against 0.794 for the stored scorers (the rule wins on 24 of 27 runs, loses on 2, p=1.0×10−5p=1.0\times 10^{-5}); on the GPT-2 runs it reaches 0.969. Current delphi removes the crop by default: the flag center_examples=True runs the un-centred windows (its branch is inverted relative to its name since delphi commit cc9387c), so only 2.8% of test peaks fall at index 24 of 32 and the fixed-index simulation prior scores −0.003-0.003. But delphi’s sampler always highlights index ℓ−⌊ℓ/4⌋=24\ell-\lfloor\ell/4\rfloor=24 in a negative, plus seeded companion marks (every negative here gets at least two). Every negative is marked at 24, against 4.3% of positives, so “yes iff index 24 is not marked” reaches 0.978 and the count rule 0.944 on items built with delphi’s code. With the flag set to False, which centres the windows, the peak sits at index 24, the fixed-index simulation prior scores 0.466, the rule at index 24 is cancelled (0.491), and the companion mark at index 31 still gives 0.994 (chosen after the fact); the count rule gives 0.935. Not preregistered: delphi draws the explanation and test examples with the same reset seed, so 10 of the 50 test examples of every feature were also shown to the explainer. SAEBench scores with centred 21-token windows (180 of 200 peaks at index 10) but shows them unmarked for detection (Karvonen et al., 2025), so no mark rule has an input.

Sequence: top-and-random simulation sets.

OpenAI’s scoring sets mix top-activating sequences with random ones (Bills et al., 2023). By Proposition 1(c), the sequence-mean predictor, which is given each sequence’s true mean activation and nothing about tokens, scores the correlation ratio η\eta, the ceiling of every rule that is constant within sequences. On our 400 neurons η\eta is 0.288 on average, above GPT-4’s published simulator (0.160). A rule reaches part of it without activations: the release lists each neuron’s five top-activating sequences first (sorted on all 400 neurons, above every later sequence on 398), and predicting 1 on those five scores 0.227, above GPT-4 on 287 of 400 neurons (p=1.5×10−18p=1.5\times 10^{-18}; post hoc). GPT-4’s simulator did not see this order, so the rule shows what the data carry, not that GPT-4 used it.

5 Does the Cue Change What the Scores Say?

A cue becomes a harm only if scores computed on the data rank features differently from scores computed without it. We tested this on the 49 features that have both stored snippets and natural windows, with Jev’s simulation scores on both (Neuronpedia stores fuzzing runs, not simulation scores) and the verdict rule written before the analysis: “harm” if the Spearman correlation of stored scores with the centre prior (ρgeo\rho_{\mathrm{geo}}) exceeds their correlation with natural-window scores (ρnat\rho_{\mathrm{nat}}) with a bootstrap interval excluding zero.

The result is adverse to the harm reading. Jev’s stored-snippet scores do track crop geometry, ρgeo=0.512\rho_{\mathrm{geo}}=0.512 [0.23, 0.72], but they track its natural-window scores more closely, ρnat=0.732\rho_{\mathrm{nat}}=0.732 [0.53, 0.87], below the split-half ceilings of the two sets (0.925 and 0.888); the difference is −0.221-0.221 [−0.52-0.52, 0.06], and the partial correlation of stored with natural scores given the centre prior is 0.710 [0.52, 0.85]. The preregistered verdict is “geometry confound present, ranking harm not shown.” What differs is the level (a paired comparison added after the preregistered test): Jev’s mean score falls from 0.478 on stored snippets to 0.331 on natural windows, lower for 44 of 49 features (p=7.6×10−9p=7.6\times 10^{-9}; Figure 3c). The two sets also differ in window length (17 against 64 tokens) and composition (5 of 25 stored snippets are non-activating; 5 of 10 natural windows are random), so this comparison does not isolate the cue; stitched passages, 74 tokens long on average and carrying a relocated centre cue, keep 0.476 (Section 6), a partial control for length only.

On the stored fuzzing runs of the first 50 features, the preregistered Spearman correlation of each scorer’s (llama-3.1-70b, gemini-1.5-flash, gemini-2.0-flash) per-feature balanced accuracy with the centre rule’s is −0.20-0.20, −0.17-0.17 and −0.19-0.19 (bootstrap intervals include zero). Outside the preregistered test, accuracy rises with the count rule’s (Spearman 0.30, 0.31 and 0.31, bootstrap intervals excluding zero; the Pearson correlations, 0.18, 0.11 and 0.19, have intervals that include zero) and, for the two Gemini scorers, with the simulation centre prior (0.42 and 0.50), which could reflect use of a cue or how sharply a feature fires. Positives with the centre unmarked, which the centre rule rejects, were accepted on 9 of 11, 9 of 11 and 10 of 11 items, against 0.69, 0.79 and 0.76 of centre-marked positives (Fisher p≥0.47p\geq 0.47; eleven items per scorer is too few to show a difference), and the 5 negatives per scorer marked at the centre were all rejected. So a score’s level here says little about the explanation, since a rule reaches it without one; the published orderings of features are not shown to be wrong, and use of the count cue is not settled.

Two further preregistered tests.

Explanation choice. We scored all 105 Neuronpedia explanations of the 49 features with Jev (2-level rubric) on both sets. The explanation that scores best on stored snippets is also best on natural windows for 36 of 49 features (chance 0.48), and 90 of 105 explanations score higher on stored snippets; but two halves of one set disagree about the best explanation (0.25, 0.31) about as often as the two sets do (0.29), so at ten windows per feature the scorer cannot resolve the ranking, and a re-ordering is neither shown nor excluded. A scorer trained on the cued data. A small encoder trained on the stored snippets of 360 features of the 500-feature sample to predict which tokens fire scores 0.526 on 100 held-out features (two seeds, Appendix C). The preregistered shortcut criterion, half the score with a blank explanation, is not met (12%); a blank explanation is out of distribution for it. The in-distribution controls say the rest: the same model trained with no explanation scores 0.438 on the same snippets (83% of the full model), a shuffled explanation keeps 31% of the full model’s score (Jev: 6%), and on natural windows the full model falls to 0.193, by 63% (Jev: 31%). Levels also matter when scores are compared across pipelines or SAEs; we did not test that.

6 Clean Data: Removing the Cues

Stitching moves the position cue.

Concatenating four stored snippets per passage and re-measuring activations on the stitched text puts the peaks at the four piece centres. A prior at the true piece centres, recovered by replaying the stitching script, scores 0.496, and Jev’s 0.476 is not above it (26 of 49 features, p=0.78p=0.78; Figure 3b); most passages were also corrupted at the byte level (Appendix F).

Random-offset natural windows remove it.

For 49 of the 50 features we computed activations locally on OpenWebText (Gokaslan & Cohen, 2019) with GPT-2 small and the same SAE, and cut 64-token windows around five activating occurrences per feature with the peak offset drawn uniformly, plus five random windows; 488 windows in total (one feature has eight). The preregistered bound was mean |r|≤0.05|r|\leq 0.05 for the centre and four-quarter priors. The centre prior scores 0.003 and the four-quarter prior −0.005-0.005 (Figure 3a,b); the best offset shared by all features, chosen after the fact over the 64 offsets (index 16), scores 0.015, and an oracle that picks the best offset separately for each feature using the true activations reaches 0.171. Because the set mixes activating and random windows, the sequence cue remains (η=0.166\eta=0.166, Figure 2); we report rwr_{w} beside it rather than remove it. A first build gave a U-shaped peak histogram and was discarded before any scoring (Appendix E).

Activations must be computed with the BOS token.

Recomputing activations locally on the stored crops without the BOS token matched Neuronpedia’s values at a median per-feature correlation of only 0.082; with it, 0.978 on the crops and 0.999 on the stitched passages. The cause is the first position’s residual outlier (Xiao et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2024): without the BOS token the first real token’s residual has 29.4 times the median norm of the others and receives a median 84% of the SAE’s activation mass (Appendix E).

Matched marks remove the fuzzing cues by construction.

By Proposition 3, if each negative’s mark set is drawn from the positives’ law independently of its label and text (e.g. the marks of a random positive of the same feature and window length, lengths drawn alike for both classes), every pre-specified mark-only rule has expected balanced accuracy 12\tfrac{1}{2}, and exactly 12\tfrac{1}{2} if the positives’ mark sets are reassigned one-to-one to as many negatives. We derived this construction and did not build or score such items.

A scorer on clean windows.

The scorer is Jev (Almeida, 2026), a commercial typed decision model (requested as jev-1.13.0; architecture and training data are not disclosed). It is an existence proof that the standard can be met, not a recommended scorer: on the simulation protocol the two open typed decision models we tried did not beat their shuffled controls (Table 1). For Jev, each token is one Score question over an ordered 10-level rubric, with the explanation and document in a shared state, and the prediction is the expected level a^s​t=∑ℓℓ​ps​t​(ℓ)\hat{a}_{st}=\sum_{\ell}\ell\,p_{st}(\ell) (Appendix C). On the natural windows it reaches a pooled correlation of 0.331 over 49 features with the 10-level rubric, against 0.013 with a shuffled explanation (46 of 49 features, p=7.0×10−11p=7.0\times 10^{-11}), above the per-feature offset oracle (38 of 49, p=1.4×10−4p=1.4\times 10^{-4}), and above the sequence-mean oracle (η=0.166\eta=0.166; 34 of 49, p=0.0094p=0.0094). By Proposition 1(b) its score splits into 0.285 within sequences and 0.045 between them, so most of it comes from ranking tokens inside a window, where the shared position priors score near zero. The same scorer’s 0.476 on stitched passages overstated its natural-window score by 0.146 (lower on natural windows for 43 of 49 features, p=5.7×10−8p=5.7\times 10^{-8}). Its cost is compared with published LLM estimates in Appendix H.

An open-weight simulator on the same windows.

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with the original all-at-once read-out on identical inputs also reads the explanation on these windows (0.194 against 0.019 shuffled; 41 of 49, p=2.0×10−6p=2.0\times 10^{-6}), at 59% of Jev’s level; it is not distinguishable from the per-feature offset oracle (25 of 49), and on the stored snippets it, like Jev, scores below the centre prior (0.386 against 0.720; Appendix C).

7 What the Sequence Cue Implies for GPT-4’s Published Simulator

On OpenAI’s release the sequence-level oracle η\eta exceeds GPT-4’s score (Section 4). We ran Jev (10-level rubric) on the 400 neurons with GPT-4’s explanations and sequences; recomputing GPT-4’s pooled correlation from its stored predictions reproduces the published score on every neuron to within 2×10−152\times 10^{-15} (a check of the pooling convention, not of the simulator), and the primary test and the wording of its outcomes were fixed after a 40-neuron pilot (Δ=+0.025\Delta=+0.025, p=0.27p=0.27) and before the run. Jev’s training data are not disclosed, so we cannot exclude that OpenAI’s release, public since 2023, was among them; the natural-window activations of Section 6 were first computed for this study and were not public before it.

Jev’s mean pooled correlation is 0.197 against GPT-4’s 0.160, a paired difference of +0.0373±0.0061+0.0373\pm 0.0061; Jev is higher on 256 of 400 neurons (p=2.3×10−8p=2.3\times 10^{-8}), the preregistered “significantly higher” outcome, which holds without the 40 pilot neurons (232 of 360, p=4.6×10−8p=4.6\times 10^{-8}; Tables 5 and 4 in Appendix I). Shuffling explanations drops Jev to 0.017 (334 wins to 66, p=3.3×10−44p=3.3\times 10^{-44}). The lead is qualified in four ways. First, it is not detected in rank correlation: mean Spearman ρ\rho is 0.074 for Jev and 0.083 for GPT-4 (p=0.051p=0.051), and for the 4-level rubric the preregistered adverse branch holds: GPT-4 is higher in rank correlation (−0.016-0.016, p=0.014p=0.014). Second, it lies mostly between sequences. Jev spreads sequence means more (η^\hat{\eta} 0.393 against 0.296); in the post hoc additive split of Proposition 1(b) the within-sequence term carries +0.010+0.010 of the +0.037+0.037 gap (235 of 400 neurons, p=5.4×10−4p=5.4\times 10^{-4}) and the between-sequence term +0.027+0.027 (260 of 400, p=2.0×10−9p=2.0\times 10^{-9}). The within-sequence correlation rwr_{w} alone is still higher for Jev (0.165 against 0.143, 242 of 400, p=3.1×10−5p=3.1\times 10^{-5}). Third, Jev sees the whole sequence, GPT-4 the prefix; restricting Jev to the causal prefix on 100 neurons changes its score from 0.185 to 0.182 (−0.0023±0.0023-0.0023\pm 0.0023; median correlation between the two predictions 0.95), an order of magnitude below the 0.037 gap, although on this subset neither variant is significantly above GPT-4 (causal p=0.13p=0.13, full context p=0.76p=0.76). Fourth, both simulators score below η\eta, so on this benchmark a sequence-level oracle outscores both and a pooled score alone cannot show token-level skill. The 8B open simulator scores 0.125 on these neurons: not resolved against GPT-4 at p=0.05p=0.05 in pooled correlation (182 of 400, p=0.08p=0.08; lower in rank correlation) and below Jev (102 of 400).

8 Limitations

Fuzzing rules on stored runs use marks rebuilt from inferred code (a wrong seed would change only the negatives’ positions), and use of a cue by a scorer is measured only through a few items and feature-level correlations, which leave the count cue unsettled (Section 5). One SAE carries stored runs at scale, the Gemma result rests on 27 runs of 12 features, and delphi items are built locally (with a BOS token delphi does not prepend). The harm test (one scorer, 49 features, one SAE) has no positive control on real data, so its sensitivity to a partial reordering is not established; “no ranking harm shown” is not “no ranking harm”. The matched-mark construction is not tested. The simulator comparison covers GPT-2 XL neurons, GPT-4 as released in 2023 and one open 8B simulator; no current closed LLM simulator was run. All Jev results were requested as jev-1.13.0 with the exact rubric wording; the API is close to, not exactly, deterministic (re-scoring identical inputs reproduced 6.5% and 9.8% of token-level values exactly, Pearson 0.997 and 0.995).

9 Conclusion

Automated-interpretability data carry the answer in their construction. A rule that reads the construction and not the explanation beats the stored LLM scorers on every stored fuzzing set we measured, and a rule reading only sequence order beats GPT-4’s published simulator (post hoc), and the cue moves between pipelines. On the data we could test, one scorer’s levels are higher on the cued data, and the cue is not shown to reorder features. Benchmarks should report the best explanation-free rule beside every score, cut windows at random offsets with the BOS token, mark negatives from the positives’ law, and report the within-sequence part of simulation scores; on such data a scorer, commercial or open, can still show that it reads the explanation.

Impact Statement

This paper concerns the reliability of automated-interpretability evaluation. We analyse public evaluation data, public models and a commercial API; no human subjects or personal data are involved, and the web-text snippets may contain offensive content. The shortcuts we describe could be used to inflate scores; we report ways to remove or separate them. This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

Appendix A Reproducibility Statement and Use of AI Assistants

Reproducibility statement.

Code, preregistrations with appended outcomes, a lab notebook, cached API responses, per-item results and a manifest with the size and SHA-256 of every input file will be released upon publication. Every number, table and figure is generated by scripts from the saved model outputs; Appendix D lists the data sources. Neuronpedia’s snippet text is replaced by content hashes (its data licence is unstated) and can be re-fetched from its public API.

Use of AI assistants.

AI assistants helped write some of the experiment code and check its correctness, helped collect public data, helped check the correctness of citations, and helped polish the paper. The three propositions restate known results; their proofs were drafted with AI assistance and checked by a separate AI pass, and the identities they state were checked numerically on the data and on random designs.

Appendix C Protocol Details

Simulation questions.

The state of one request holds the explanation, a note (“Each document is written as <index>‹token›; whitespace inside the brackets is part of the token”) and the document rendered as <0>‹ edit›<1>‹ ]›…. Each token is one Score question whose instructions are the object {document, token_index, token}, with one of the rubrics below; the read-out is the returned expected level only, and the reported confidence is not used.

  • •

    10 levels: “0 - nothing to do with the description”, “1 - a very faint, incidental connection”, “2 - a weak connection”, “3 - a mild connection”, “4 - a moderate connection”, “5 - a clear connection”, “6 - a clear and direct instance”, “7 - a strong, central instance”, “8 - a very strong, textbook instance”, “9 - the strongest possible instance of the description”.

  • •

    4 levels: “0 - not the described thing”, “1 - weakly or indirectly related”, “2 - clearly the described thing”, “3 - the strongest possible instance of the description”.

  • •

    2 levels: “0 - not the described thing”, “1 - the described thing”.

The API accepts at most 10 levels, so GPT-4’s 0–10 becomes 0–9. By Proposition 1(a) the change of numeric range does not matter; the change from eleven levels to ten is a change of rubric, which (a) does not cover (the 2-, 4- and 10-level rubrics are compared in Table 2). The “bare index” arms render all tokens of the batch as one <n>‹token› stream and use the integer nn as the question’s only instruction. The “terse” arm uses ten bare numerals as criteria and moves the level wording into the state.

Detection and fuzzing questions.

The state holds the explanation and the excerpts as plain text. Each excerpt gets one Noul (yes/no) question asking whether it contains at least one token the feature would fire on, with the two criteria “at least one token in this excerpt is an instance of what explanation describes” and “no token in this excerpt is an instance of what explanation describes”. Fuzzing wraps marked tokens in << >> and asks whether the marked tokens are instances of the explanation, thresholded at 0.5 before the run.

Batching and latency.

Production runs used batches of up to 70 questions per request and eight concurrent workers. On the 400-neuron run (4,399 requests, 63.7 questions per request on average) the measured median latency was 1.15 s and the 95th percentile 2.93 s per request, read from the run’s usage record. The vendor’s documented limit of 1,200 requests per minute binds beyond about 23 workers.

Explanation-choice test.

All 105 Neuronpedia explanations of the 49 natural-window features (43 features carry two, 5 three, 1 four) were scored by Jev under one protocol on the paper’s stored snippets and on the natural windows, with the 2-level rubric as the preregistered primary and the 10-level rubric secondary. Best-explanation agreement is the fraction of features whose top explanation coincides across the two sets; the split-half disagreement draws 2,000 stratified half-splits of each set’s windows and reports how often the two halves disagree about the best explanation within a set, and between a half of each set. Re-scoring the paper’s explanation with the 10-level rubric on identical inputs reproduced 6.5% (stored) and 9.8% (natural) of token-level values exactly, Pearson 0.997 and 0.995.

Trained scorer.

A 22.7M-parameter sentence encoder (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) with a linear token head reads [CLS] explanation [SEP] snippet [SEP] and is trained with binary cross-entropy to predict whether each GPT-2 token fires (activation above zero), on the stored snippets of 360 features of the 500-feature sample (40 more for epoch selection, 100 held out), for 6 epochs and two seeds (held-out scores differ by less than 0.01 between seeds). Each GPT-2 token’s target and prediction attach to the first word piece overlapping its span. The no-explanation arm is the same model trained with the explanation blank. Scores are the per-feature pooled Pearson correlation of the sigmoid output with the raw activations, averaged over features.

Open-weight simulator.

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with the prompt of OpenAI’s all-at-once simulator (system message, three few-shot records and the target sequence as a prefilled assistant turn with every activation unknown), rendered through the model’s chat template; at each unknown slot the prompt log-probabilities over the digit tokens 0–10 are renormalised and their expected value is the simulated activation. One forward pass per sequence, nothing generated; 11,590 sequences (the 400 OpenAI neurons, the 49 natural windows and the 49 features’ stored snippets, each with the feature’s and a shuffled explanation). The preregistered top-20 log-probabilities failed 21 of the 100 OpenAI sequences of the smoke run (a slot with no digit among the top 20 fails the whole sequence), so the full run used the top 100, decided before it started; 88 sequences still failed and were dropped, never zero-filled, and every unit kept at least nine of its ten documents. Inference took 2 h 10 min on one H200; the mean GPU utilisation was 4.6%, since the engine post-processes the top-100 prompt log-probabilities on the CPU. Reading the eleven digit logits at the slot positions directly would avoid this.

Harm-test control.

After the real-data result, the preregistered rule of Section 5 was run on synthetic rankings of 49 features (post hoc): with stored scores built from the crop geometry alone plus noise it returned “harm demonstrated”; built from the natural-window scores alone, “no ranking harm shown”; mixing the two, it first fired at a geometry weight of 0.6 (4 of 5 seeds) and from 0.7 in every seed. This calibrates the instrument on synthetic data and is not a positive control on real data.

Appendix D Data Sources

Neuronpedia’s stored runs (GPT-2 small layer 8: 500 random features, plus the first 50 features in index order, each with the explanation and the 25 snippets of its stored fuzzing runs, where runs cover more than one explanation the one with the most runs; Gemma-2-2B layer 20: 12 features) and the activations of the stitched passages were obtained from its public API in September 2026 (Lin, 2023). The delphi items were built with EleutherAI/delphi at commit 4fea06e (EleutherAI, 2024) and SAEBench’s scoring windows with SAEBench at commit 8042bb3 (Karvonen et al., 2025), both on the 10k-document OpenWebText subset (OpenWebText-10k). The 400 GPT-2 XL neurons come from OpenAI’s public release (Bills et al., 2023). The natural windows and the BOS recomputations use GPT-2 small and the same SAE (Bloom, 2024), run locally with the BOS token. The fork version behind Neuronpedia’s stored runs is inferred, since its dependency lock pins no revision; the three files involved did not change in their marking logic after November 2024.

Appendix E Preregistrations and Their Outcomes

Extension to 400 neurons.

Written after the 40-neuron pilot and before the extension ran: per-neuron pooled rr, Jev 10-level minus GPT-4 published, sign test, with three outcomes worded in advance; no exclusion, no rubric choice after the fact, no change of pooling. Outcome: significantly higher.

Follow-up analyses.

Two sets of follow-ups were preregistered with decision rules before they ran, and their outcomes appended without editing the rules (in the preregistration file, to be released with the code). The first: rank correlation, sequence-level terms, pilot exclusion, Holm correction and equivalence intervals; the fuzzing position and count rules; BOS versus context in the local recompute; natural windows; the exact piece-centre prior; the causal-prefix and 2-level-rubric checks; and a current LLM simulator, which was not run. The second: the harm test of Section 5; the delphi and SAEBench builds; the 500-feature analysis on Neuronpedia; and small recomputes (equivalence on rebuilt marks, the natural-window split, the chunking of the natural windows, the first BOS-less attempt, the BOS mechanism). The decision rules and verdicts: harm, “geometry confound present, ranking harm not shown”; 500-feature sample, “leak replicates” on GPT-2 (the same rebuild rule on 500 further features) and “no position leak” on Gemma (the preregistrations’ “leak” is this paper’s cue), with the count rule reported regardless; delphi default, “no fixed-offset leak in simulation” and a fuzzing position cue above the 0.6 bound; BOS mechanism, “stated as measured”; rank correlation, “does not separate them” for the 10-level rubric and, for the 4-level rubric, “GPT-4 is higher on rank correlation” (Spearman −0.016-0.016, p=0.014p=0.014; Table 5). The first BOS-less attempt used a subsample of 8 features and 8 snippets (0.138, against 0.082 on all features). Without the BOS token, dropping the first position restores a median correlation of 0.985, and centring each position’s residual restores 0.994 with the norm ratio unchanged.

Third set.

Written before each item ran, outcomes appended: the explanation-choice test (rule: best-explanation disagreement of at least 0.25 between the two sets with the split-half test at p<0.05p<0.05; outcome “not shown”, with the instrument flag that the scorer cannot resolve the ranking at this sample size; the 10-level rubric, run as the secondary arm, gives 37 of 49 features and 93 of 105 explanations); the trained scorer (rule: at least half the score kept with a blank explanation and at least half lost on natural windows, on the two-seed mean; outcome “not shown”, the first clause failing at 12%); and the open-weight simulator (rule: above its shuffled control on the natural windows with a sign test at p<0.05p<0.05; outcome “reads the explanation”, instrument sensitive on the OpenAI neurons; lower than Jev on all three sets; against GPT-4 not resolved in pooled correlation and lower in rank correlation). Its one deviation, the top-100 log-probabilities, was decided on the smoke run before the full run (Appendix C).

Not preregistered.

The train/test overlap in delphi, found while replicating its sampler; the paired level comparison and the count-rule and simulation-centre-prior correlations of the stored fuzzing accuracy (Section 5); the offset shared by all features on the natural windows, computed after the preregistered natural-window analyses (Section 6); the additive within/between split of Section 7; the centre prior and η\eta on the 50 stored-snippet features and the 400 OpenAI neurons, computed before the follow-up preregistrations; and two analyses of existing outputs, each recorded as post hoc in the preregistration file: the sequence-order rule on OpenAI’s release and the centre rule with uniformly random negative mark positions (Section 4).

Deviations for the natural windows.

All three were fixed before any Jev call: the corpus was read from the loader’s source archive; documents were truncated to 1,016 tokens and cut into 127-token chunks, each run with the BOS token as a 128-token context (the SAE’s training length), so every window has at most 127 tokens of left context; and a first build that drew each offset from the occurrence’s feasible range gave a U-shaped peak histogram and was discarded before scoring.

Open typed decision models.

Preregistered before running: both 1,024-token Laya checkpoints, laya-typed-decisions (421M) and laya-multilingual (322M), on the 400 neurons with byte-identical inputs. Both fell below GPT-4 and were indistinguishable from their own shuffled controls (Table 1); a rendering change tested with a written rule did not repair them. We draw no conclusion about typed decision models as a category.

Appendix F Stitched Passages

Each passage concatenates four snippets in a seeded random order, one to three from the feature (cycling with the passage index) and the rest from other features, and its activations come from Neuronpedia’s activation endpoint on the stitched text: 49 features, 392 passages. Each feature gets eight passages; one of the 50 features has fewer than three activating snippets and was skipped. The peaks sit at the four piece centres, so a prior at the true centres scores 0.496. Snippet tokens were joined as text and re-tokenised by the endpoint, and 359 of the 392 passages contain byte-level mojibake. The rubric ablation below was run on this set; the comparison of the 10- and 4-level rubrics does not survive Holm correction.

Appendix G Detection and Fuzzing on the First 50 Features

On rebuilt marks Jev’s fuzzing accuracy is equivalent to llama-3.1-70b’s within 0.05 (difference +0.0065+0.0065, 90% interval [−0.035,0.048][-0.035,0.048]), and both are below the centre and count rules. These comparisons are on items that carry the cues of Section 4, so they order scorers on the same data but do not measure explanation quality.

Appendix H Cost

Jev bills input tokens only, but a per-token protocol re-sends the rubric with every token: 69.3 input tokens per token scored with the 2-level rubric and 165.3 with the 10-level one. The literature’s costs for Llama-70b scorers (Paulo et al., 2025) are estimates for 100 contexts per feature. At that budget with 32-token contexts, Jev simulation costs $931 per 100k features with the 2-level rubric against an estimated $3,600 for all-at-once simulation, a factor of 3.9, and $2,222 with the 10-level rubric, a factor of 1.6; detection costs $58 against an estimated $588, a factor of 10.1. At 200 contexts the 10-level rubric costs $4,443 per 100k features, 1.23 times the 100-context estimate, that is, more than the LLM; since that estimate is for half the budget, the same-budget factors above are the comparison. The 2-level rubric is weaker on neurons: above GPT-4 (+0.0187+0.0187, p=5.4×10−4p=5.4\times 10^{-4}) but below the 10-level rubric (−0.0186-0.0186, p=7.1×10−9p=7.1\times 10^{-9}; Table 5). Table 4 projects whole dictionaries at the 640-token budget of Bills et al. (2023) with the 2-level rubric.
